extracted.intended_audience: student journalists and general readers interested in media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/editorial assessing journalistic practices in coverage of the Hasan Minhaj controversy, focused on fact-checking, sourcing, framing, and harm-minimization. Useful as guidance for student journalists and readers evaluating media coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy as core duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy is at the core of journalism; reporters have a duty to faithfully represent what sources tell them to minimize harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always prioritize factual accuracy even in 'small stakes' stories; misrepresentation can harm individuals and communities (e.g., avoid misrepresenting quotes or facts about Hasan Minhaj or Trinity community members).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must verify the facts they publish and be careful in asserting factual claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure thorough fact-checking before publication; dispute over whether the New Yorker 'carefully fact-checked' Minhaj's anecdotes illustrates why verification matters. If fact-checking is limited, avoid strong factual assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and justify anonymous sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying heavily on anonymous sources can make an article seem unreliable; use named sources when possible and justify anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If most sources are unnamed (the article notes 20+ people interviewed with the 'vast majority' anonymous), explain why anonymity is necessary and balance with named attribution in relatively low-stakes profiles or cultural pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful quoting and context preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes should be presented in context; paraphrasing must not change the original meaning of a source's words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid paraphrases or rewordings that alter a speaker's intent (example: paraphrasing Minhaj's account to imply he 'faked racism' when his meaning differed). When in doubt, use direct quotes or clarify paraphrase choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful framing and language choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Word choice and framing should not imply conclusions beyond the evidence (e.g., saying 'much' of anecdotes 'never happened' implies a majority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise language; avoid subtle rhetorical moves that overstate findings. If evidence is partial, qualify claims rather than implying broad culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: If critiquing a practice (such as fabrication in comedy), place individual cases in broader context rather than isolating one subject unfairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing common practices (e.g., many comedians 'fudge' stories), contextualize an individual's behavior within industry norms and avoid making one person the sole exemplar unless justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality and prioritization of issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Give attention proportionate to the seriousness of the issues uncovered; higher-stakes matters should receive more focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, workplace issues faced by female staff on 'Patriot Act' may merit more scrutiny than anecdote fabrication; editorial judgment should prioritize harm and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid manipulating information to fit a narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not shape or manipulate gathered information to tell a preselected side of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the urge to craft a dramatic narrative at the expense of nuance; present competing accounts and ambiguities rather than force-fitting facts into a single storyline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about errors and corrections process
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications should acknowledge mistakes, provide correction mechanisms, and invite reader input to fix errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage readers to submit corrections or letters to the editor (the Trinitonian describes inviting corrections and providing instructions in print), and publish corrections visibly when errors are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of genre conventions (comedic license)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on comedic performances, account for storytelling conventions where comedians may change chronology or details for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between deceptive factual claims and common rhetorical or comedic devices (e.g., Minhaj changing timing of a prom rejection for effect). Reporting should note such conventions when assessing truthfulness or harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and display of facts matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The way facts are displayed in an article can alter reader perception; presentation should preserve nuance and proportionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond factual accuracy, structure and emphasis (which quotes are foregrounded, which allegations are highlighted) should fairly reflect the balance of evidence and importance of issues raised.
